variants.stem: The 24-hour PM2.5 value reported each hour hardly changes from one hour to the next, yet a fire nearby can make the air much worse within an hour. Explain why the 24-hour value changes slowly and why the 1-hour value is sometimes reported as well.
variants.explanation: The 24-hour value is an average of the present hourly reading and the previous 23, so one new hour changes it by only about 1/24 of the difference. The 1-hour value tracks the present, so it shows a sudden event (haze, fire) that the 24-hour value would take many hours to reflect.

rubric.criterion: The 24-hour value is an average of the latest and the previous 23 hourly values, so one new hour moves it only a little
The 1-hour value responds quickly to a sudden change such as haze or a fire, so it is reported when conditions are changing

variants.perspectiveLabel: Reasons the PSI descriptors may mislead (4 marks)
variants.stem: The PSI descriptor ("moderate", "unhealthy") is sometimes read as a direct statement about health. Give **four** reasons it can mislead.
variants.hint: Think about where the bands come from, what the number leaves out, and what it does not say about time.
variants.explanation: The health thresholds are extrapolated from studies with assumptions; the number gives no uncertainty; it ignores what the particles are made of (cigarette smoke is mostly carbon and tar, haze particles carry metals and other material); it has no time dimension (the exposure that matters is cumulative) and an equivalence with smoking compares unlike particles.

rubric.criterion: The bands rest on extrapolated health data and assumptions
No error analysis or uncertainty is attached to the number
It ignores the composition of the particles (carbon and tar versus metals and industrial particles)
No time dimension: short exposure and long cumulative exposure are not distinguished

The selectivity factor is the ratio of the two retention factors, α = k_B/k_A = {{fix(al,2)}} (the same as the ratio of the adjusted times t_S). α = 1 would mean no separation.

metadata.title: Resolution of two peaks
metadata.source: Chromatography slides; booklet (efficiency and band spreading)

variants.perspectiveLabel: R_S from baseline widths and a verdict (4 marks)
variants.stem: Two peaks have retention times **{{fix(tA,2)}} min** and **{{fix(tB,2)}} min** and baseline widths **{{fix(WA,2)}} min** and **{{fix(WB,2)}} min**. Calculate the resolution R_S and say how well the peaks are separated.
variants.hint: R_S = 2 (t_B − t_A)/(W_A + W_B). R_S < 1.0 poor, about 1.0 partial, ≥ 1.5 baseline separation.
variants.explanation: R_S = 2({{fix(tB,2)}} − {{fix(tA,2)}})/({{fix(WA,2)}} + {{fix(WB,2)}}) = {{fix(rs,2)}}. Resolution depends on both the distance between the peaks and their widths. Below 1.0 the peaks overlap noticeably, about 1.0 they just touch, and 1.5 or more is baseline separation.

paths.label: The factor 2 is missing: R_S = 2(t_B − t_A)/(W_A + W_B).
Use the mean width: the sum of the widths goes in the denominator with a factor 2 in the numerator.

variants.stem: Two peaks elute at **{{fix(tA,2)}} min** and **{{fix(tB,2)}} min**. Their widths at half height are **{{fix(hA,2)}} min** and **{{fix(hB,2)}} min**. Calculate R_S.
variants.hint: Half-height widths use the booklet form R_S = 1.178 (t_B − t_A)/(w½A + w½B), not the one with 2.
variants.explanation: When the widths are measured at half height the constant is 1.178 (it converts w½ to the baseline width W = 1.699 w½): R_S = 1.178({{fix(tB,2)}} − {{fix(tA,2)}})/({{fix(hA,2)}} + {{fix(hB,2)}}) = {{fix(rs,2)}}.

paths.label: That is the form for baseline widths (factor 2). With half-height widths use 1.178.

variants.perspectiveLabel: What a change in width does to R_S (4 marks)
variants.stem: Two peaks elute at **{{fix(tA,2)}} min** and **{{fix(tB,2)}} min** with baseline widths **{{fix(WA,2)}} min** and **{{fix(WB,2)}} min**. Calculate R_S. A different column makes **both** peaks **{{fix(p,0)}}% wider** with the same retention times. What is the new R_S?
variants.hint: R_S = 2 (t_B − t_A)/(W_A + W_B). Both widths scale by (1 + p/100).
variants.explanation: R_S = {{fix(rs,2)}}. Widening both peaks by {{fix(p,0)}}% multiplies the denominator by {{fix(f,2)}} while the separation of the peak centres is unchanged, so R_S falls to {{fix(rs2,2)}}: resolution depends on the width as well as the distance between the peaks.

paths.label: The factor 2 is missing: R_S = 2(t_B − t_A)/(W_A + W_B).
R_S falls when the peaks widen: divide by (1 + p/100), do not multiply.

ecf.label: Consistent with your own R_S.

variants.stem: A column of length **{{fix(L,0)}} cm** gives R_S = **{{fix(R1,2)}}** for a pair of solutes. (a) What R_S would you expect from a column of the same kind and **{{fix(g,0)}} times the length**? (b) What length would you need to reach **R_S = {{fix(Rt,1)}}**?
variants.hint: R_S ∝ √N and N ∝ L at fixed H, so R_S ∝ √L.
variants.explanation: Resolution grows with the square root of the plate number, and N = L/H, so R_S ∝ √L. Multiplying the length by {{fix(g,0)}} multiplies R_S by √{{fix(g,0)}}: {{fix(R2,2)}}. To reach R_S = {{fix(Rt,1)}} the length must change by (R_t/R_S)² = {{fix(q,2)}}: L = {{fix(L2,0)}} cm. Doubling R_S takes four times the length (and about four times the time).

fields.label: Length needed for the target R_S

paths.label: R_S grows as the square root of L, not in proportion to L.
Length goes as the square of the R_S ratio (R_S ∝ √L), not linearly.

metadata.title: Plate number N and plate height H
metadata.source: Chromatography slides; booklet (efficiency and band spreading)

variants.perspectiveLabel: N and H from a baseline width (4 marks)
variants.stem: A peak elutes at **{{fix(tR,2)}} min** and has a baseline width of **{{fix(W,2)}} min** on a column **{{fix(L,2)}} m** long. Calculate the number of theoretical plates N and the plate height H (in mm).
variants.hint: N = 16 (t_R/W)². H = L/N.
variants.explanation: N = 16({{fix(tR,2)}}/{{fix(W,2)}})² = {{fix(N,0)}} plates. H = L/N = {{fix(H,3)}} mm. A smaller H and a larger N mean a more efficient column.

paths.label: N goes as the square of t_R/W.
The constant 5.55 belongs to the half-height width; with the baseline width use 16.
H = L/N with L in mm.

ecf.label: Consistent with your own N.

variants.perspectiveLabel: N from a half-height width (3 marks)
variants.stem: A peak elutes at **{{fix(tR,2)}} min** with a width at half height of **{{fix(h,3)}} min** on a column **{{fix(L,2)}} m** long. Calculate N and H (in µm).
variants.hint: With the half-height width the booklet gives N = 5.55 (t_R/w½)².

paths.label: With the half-height width the constant is 5.55, not 16.

ecf.label: Consistent with your own N.

variants.perspectiveLabel: Plates and length needed for a target R_S (6 marks)
variants.stem: A pair of solutes has **α = {{fix(al,2)}}** and **k_B = {{fix(kB,1)}}**. The column's plate height is **{{fix(Hmm,2)}} mm**. How many plates are needed for **R_S = {{fix(Rt,1)}}**, and how long must the column be?
variants.hint: Purnell: R_S = (√N/4)((α − 1)/α)(k_B/(1 + k_B)). Solve for N, then L = N × H.
variants.explanation: Solving the Purnell equation for N: N = 16 R_S² (α/(α − 1))² ((1 + k_B)/k_B)² = {{fix(N,0)}} plates. L = N × H = {{fix(N,0)}} × {{fix(Hmm,2)}} mm = {{fix(L,0)}} mm. The selectivity term (α − 1)/α is the most sensitive: a small α needs a very long column.

paths.label: Leave out the retention term: N = 16 R_S² (α/(α−1))² ((1 + k_B)/k_B)².
The terms are squared: R_S, α/(α−1) and (1 + k_B)/k_B all appear squared.

ecf.label: Consistent with your own N.

variants.perspectiveLabel: R_S from N, α and k (4 marks)
variants.stem: A column with **N = {{fix(N,0)}} plates** separates two solutes with **α = {{fix(al,2)}}** and **k_B = {{fix(kB,1)}}**. Calculate R_S. Then find the R_S if the column is replaced by one with **four times as many plates**.
variants.explanation: R_S = (√{{fix(N,0)}}/4)(({{fix(al,2)}} − 1)/{{fix(al,2)}})({{fix(kB,1)}}/(1 + {{fix(kB,1)}})) = {{fix(rs,2)}}. Four times the plates doubles R_S (it goes as √N), giving {{fix(rs4,2)}}.

fields.label: R_S with four times the plates

paths.label: Check the selectivity term: it is (α − 1)/α.
R_S goes as √N, so four times the plates doubles it, not quadruples it.

ecf.label: Consistent with your own R_S.

metadata.title: Linear velocity, volume flow and scale-up
metadata.source: Chromatography slides; booklet (efficiency and band spreading)

variants.perspectiveLabel: Linear velocity in a packed column (3 marks)
variants.stem: A packed column has an inner diameter of **{{fix(d,2)}} cm**. The fraction of the column volume the mobile phase can occupy is **ε = {{fix(eps,2)}}**. The volume flow rate is **{{fix(uv,2)}} mL min⁻¹**. Calculate the linear velocity u_x (cm min⁻¹).
variants.hint: Volume flow u_v = u_x π r² ε for a packed column, r = d/2.
variants.explanation: The cross-section open to flow is π r² ε with r = d/2 = {{fix(d/2,2)}} cm, so u_x = u_v/(π r² ε) = {{fix(ux,2)}} cm min⁻¹ (1 mL = 1 cm³).

paths.label: Use the radius (half the inner diameter) in π r².
Only the fraction ε of the cross-section carries the flow: divide by ε as well.

variants.stem: An analytical column of inner diameter **{{fix(d1,1)}} cm** handles **{{fix(m1,0)}} mg** of sample at **{{fix(F1,1)}} mL min⁻¹**. You want to purify **{{fix(m2,0)}} mg** per run on a column of the same length and packing, at the same linear velocity. What inner diameter and what volume flow do you need?
variants.hint: Sample capacity scales with the cross-sectional area (∝ d²). At the same linear velocity the volume flow scales with the same factor.
variants.explanation: The mass ratio is {{fix(q,1)}}, and capacity ∝ area ∝ d², so d₂ = d₁ √{{fix(q,1)}} = {{fix(d2,2)}} cm. The same linear velocity through {{fix(q,1)}} times the area needs {{fix(q,1)}} times the volume flow: {{fix(F2,2)}} mL min⁻¹. Length and linear velocity are unchanged, so the separation is unchanged.

paths.label: Capacity goes as the cross-sectional area, so the diameter scales as the square root of the mass ratio.
Keep the same linear velocity: the volume flow scales with the area, which is the mass ratio.

metadata.title: Band spreading and the van Deemter equation
metadata.source: Chromatography slides; booklet (efficiency and band spreading)

variants.perspectiveLabel: Which term is multiple flow paths
variants.stem: In H = A + B/u + C u, which term describes **multiple flow paths** (eddy diffusion) through a packed column?
variants.explanation: A is the multiple-paths term, independent of flow rate; B/u is longitudinal diffusion and C u is the finite time to equilibrate between phases (mass transfer).

options.label: None: it is part of all three

variants.stem: At a flow velocity **below the optimum**, which term dominates the plate height?
variants.explanation: At low velocity the solute spends longer in the column and diffuses along it, so B/u dominates. Above the optimum, the time to equilibrate matters more and C u dominates; at the optimum B/u and C u contribute equally and H is smallest.

options.label: None: H is flat below the optimum

variants.stem: At a flow velocity **above the optimum**, which term dominates?
variants.explanation: Fast flow leaves too little time for the solute to equilibrate between mobile and stationary phases, so the C u (mass-transfer) term grows and H rises.

options.label: C u: the solute cannot equilibrate between the phases fast enough

variants.perspectiveLabel: Longitudinal diffusion in GC and LC
variants.stem: Which statement about longitudinal diffusion is correct?
variants.explanation: The B/u term contains the diffusion coefficient of the solute in the mobile phase. Diffusion is far faster in a gas, so B/u is larger in GC (worst at low flow).

options.label: It is larger in GC than in LC because diffusion in a gas is much faster than in a liquid
It contributes equally in GC and LC
It is larger in LC because liquids are denser

variants.perspectiveLabel: The A term in an open tubular column
variants.stem: Why can the A term be taken as zero for an open tubular GC column?
variants.explanation: Multiple flow paths come from the packing particles. An open tube has one path down the middle, so A ≈ 0.

options.label: There is a single open flow path, so there are no multiple paths around packing particles
The stationary phase film is thin

variants.stem: At the optimum flow velocity of the van Deemter curve:
variants.explanation: dH/du = 0 gives u_opt = √(B/C). There B/u = C u, plate height is lowest and the column is most efficient.

options.label: H is a minimum, so N is a maximum, and B/u and C u are equal
H is a maximum and N a minimum
B/u and C u are both zero

variants.perspectiveLabel: Three causes of band broadening and how to reduce each (6 marks)
variants.stem: Name the **three** main causes of band broadening in a column and give one way of reducing **each**.
variants.explanation: Multiple flow paths (A): different molecules take paths of different length through the packing; use small, uniform particles and pack well. Longitudinal diffusion (B/u): the band spreads along the column by diffusion, worst at low flow and in gases; run near or above the optimum velocity. Finite equilibration time, or mass transfer (C u): molecules cannot equilibrate between the phases instantly, worst at high flow; use a slower flow, smaller particles or a thinner stationary-phase film.

rubric.criterion: Multiple flow paths (eddy diffusion), the A term
Reduce it with small particles of a narrow size range packed uniformly
Longitudinal diffusion along the column, the B/u term
Reduce it by using a faster flow (less time to diffuse)
Finite time to equilibrate between phases (mass transfer), the C u term
Reduce it with a slower flow, smaller particles or a thinner film

metadata.title: Peak shape and what it tells you
metadata.source: Chromatography slides; booklet (efficiency and band spreading)

variants.stem: Which is the most common cause of a **fronting** peak?
variants.explanation: Fronting is classically an overload effect. Tailing, by contrast, usually comes from some molecules being held too strongly (for example by silanol groups or active sites). Neither is caused by mobile-phase velocity alone.

options.label: Overloading the column: too much analyte, so part of the band is retained less strongly and comes out early
Residual silanol groups holding some molecules more strongly
A mobile phase velocity that is too high

variants.stem: Which is a common cause of a **tailing** peak in HPLC on a silica-based column?
variants.explanation: Secondary interactions with residual Si–OH groups hold some molecules more strongly, so they come out late. End-capping (trimethylsilyl groups), a different pH or mobile phase, or a smaller injection reduce tailing.

options.label: Some molecules interact strongly with residual silanol groups and are released late
A flow velocity that is exactly optimum
A column that is too long

variants.stem: The asymmetry factor A/B is measured at 10% of the peak height. A peak has **A/B > 1**. What does that show?
variants.explanation: In the lecture convention A/B > 1 is tailing and A/B < 1 is fronting; a symmetric peak has A/B = 1. The 10%-height measurement also enters the plate-count formula N ≈ 41.7 (t_R/w₀.₁)²/(A/B + 1.25).

variants.stem: A peak shows fronting on a non-polar (reversed-phase) column. Assume the usual cause. Which change is most likely to help?
variants.explanation: On a non-polar column the usual cause of fronting is overload: too much analyte saturates the retention sites, so part of the band is retained less strongly and comes out early. The fix is to inject less or dilute the sample. Silanol groups are the cause of tailing (some molecules held too strongly), so adding them would not cure fronting. A longer column only adds plates; it does not change the overload.

options.label: Inject a smaller amount or a more dilute sample
Use a longer column of the same kind
Add more free silanol groups to the packing

metadata.title: Types of chromatography and general rules
metadata.source: Chromatography slides; booklet (efficiency and band spreading)

variants.stem: In **size-exclusion** chromatography, which molecules elute first?
variants.explanation: Large molecules are excluded from the pores and pass straight through; small ones enter the pores and are delayed.

options.label: The largest: they cannot enter the pores and take the shortest path

variants.stem: In any chromatographic separation, which solute is detected **first**?
variants.explanation: The separation exploits different rates of movement. The solute that spends more of its time in the mobile phase moves faster and elutes first.

options.label: The one with more affinity for the mobile phase (less retained)
The one with more affinity for the stationary phase

variants.stem: A more hydrophobic solute is retained longer on a reversed-phase column. Is the hold-up (void) time t_M longer for it?
variants.explanation: t_R = t_M + t_S. The retention of a solute lengthens t_S, not t_M, which is the time of an unretained compound.

options.label: No: t_M is a property of the column and conditions, the same for every solute

variants.stem: Which mechanism does **ion-exchange** chromatography use?
variants.explanation: Ion exchange: fixed charges on the stationary phase retain oppositely charged solute ions. Partition uses a liquid film, size exclusion uses pores, and affinity uses a specific binding partner.

options.label: Fixed charged groups on the packing attract counter-ions from the sample
A liquid film on a solid support dissolves the solute
Specific binding to an attached antibody

variants.stem: Which description fits **affinity** chromatography?
variants.explanation: Affinity is the most selective mode: a specific binder (for example an antibody) is bonded to the support, and the bound analyte is released by changing the pH or ionic strength.

options.label: The stationary phase carries a group that binds the analyte specifically; it is released by changing pH or ionic strength
It needs a gaseous mobile phase

variants.stem: In the Purnell equation the retention term k_B/(1 + k_B) is about 0.5 at k_B = 1, 0.83 at 5 and 0.91 at 10. What does that tell you about increasing k?
variants.explanation: The term levels off towards 1: beyond k of about 5 the extra retention buys almost no resolution and costs time and peak height.

options.label: Raising k beyond about 5 gains little resolution but lengthens the run
Resolution rises in proportion to k
k has no effect on resolution

metadata.title: ISE calibration with a dilution chain
metadata.source: Topic 3b · calibration with a dilution chain (finals style)

variants.perspectiveLabel: K⁺ electrode: calibration line and two dilutions (8 marks)
variants.stem:
A K⁺ ion-selective electrode is calibrated with standards made up in a constant background electrolyte, so concentration can be used in place of activity:

| c (M) | E (mV) |
|---|---|
| 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ | {{fix(E1,1)}} |
| 1.0 × 10⁻³ | {{fix(Em,1)}} |
| 1.0 × 10⁻² | {{fix(E3,1)}} |

A serum sample is diluted in two steps: **{{fix(Va,0)}} mL** is made up to **{{fix(Vb,0)}} mL**, then **{{fix(Vc,0)}} mL** of that solution is made up to **{{fix(Vd,0)}} mL**. The final solution gives **{{fix(Ex,1)}} mV**. Use the line through the two end standards.

(a) Find the slope of the calibration (mV per decade).
(b) Find log c for the final solution, and its concentration.
(c) What is the overall dilution factor?
(d) What is the K⁺ concentration of the original serum?
variants.hint: Slope = (E at 10⁻² M − E at 10⁻⁴ M)/2 decades. log c = −4 + (E − E₁)/slope with E₁ the reading at 10⁻⁴ M. Dilution factor = (V_b/V_a) × (V_d/V_c); multiply the measured concentration by it.
variants.explanation: The two end standards are two decades apart, so the slope is (E₃ − E₁)/2 = {{fix(sl,2)}} mV per decade (close to the Nernstian 59 mV for a cation). A reading is converted by log c = −4 + (E − E₁)/slope = {{fix(lgx,2)}}, so the measured solution holds ${{sci(cx,2)}}$ M. Each dilution divides the concentration, so the original is the measured value times both factors: ({{fix(Vb,0)}}/{{fix(Va,0)}}) × ({{fix(Vd,0)}}/{{fix(Vc,0)}}) = {{fix(DF,1)}}, giving ${{sci(c0,2)}}$ M. Constant ionic strength is what lets concentration replace activity.

fields.label: log c of the final solution

paths.label: The end standards are two decades apart: divide the potential difference by 2.

ecf.label: Consistent with your own slope.
Consistent with your own log c.

paths.label: Both dilutions count: multiply (V_b/V_a) by (V_d/V_c).
The dilution factor is final volume over the volume taken, not the reverse.
The measured solution is dilute: multiply by the dilution factor to get back to the original, not divide.
Both dilution steps must be undone, not just the first.

ecf.label: Consistent with your own concentration and dilution factor.

variants.perspectiveLabel: Ammonia probe in a Kjeldahl analysis: calibration, dilution and weight % N (10 marks)
variants.stem:
An ammonia gas-sensing electrode (its potential falls as the NH₃ concentration rises) is calibrated with standards in a constant background:

| c (M) | E (mV) |
|---|---|
| 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ | {{fix(E1,1)}} |
| 1.0 × 10⁻³ | {{fix(Em,1)}} |
| 1.0 × 10⁻² | {{fix(E3,1)}} |

A **{{fix(m,2)}} g** food sample is digested by the Kjeldahl method, made alkaline and made up to **{{fix(Vt,0)}} mL**. **{{fix(Va,0)}} mL** of this solution is diluted to **{{fix(Vb,0)}} mL** and gives **{{fix(Ex,1)}} mV**. Use the line through the two end standards.

(a) Find the slope of the calibration.
(b) Find log c and the NH₃ concentration of the diluted solution.
(c) What was the concentration in the {{fix(Vt,0)}} mL solution?
(d) How many mg of nitrogen does the sample contain (N = 14.01 g mol⁻¹)?
(e) What is the weight percent nitrogen in the food?
variants.hint: Slope = (E at 10⁻² M − E at 10⁻⁴ M)/2; for a gas probe it is negative. log c = −4 + (E − E₁)/slope. Undo the dilution (× V_b/V_a), then n(N) = c × V_t, mass = n × 14.01, % N = mass/sample mass × 100.
variants.explanation: Slope = (E₃ − E₁)/2 = {{fix(sl,2)}} mV per decade (negative for a gas probe whose reading falls as NH₃ rises). log c = −4 + (E − E₁)/slope = {{fix(lgx,2)}}, so the diluted solution holds ${{sci(cm,2)}}$ M. Undoing the dilution: ${{sci(cd,2)}}$ M in the {{fix(Vt,0)}} mL. Moles of N = c × V = {{fix(nN * 1000,2)}} mmol, so {{fix(mN,1)}} mg of nitrogen, which is {{fix(pct,1)}}% of the {{fix(m,2)}} g sample. Each mole of nitrogen in the protein gives one mole of NH₃, which is why moles of NH₃ equal moles of N.

fields.label: log c of the diluted solution

paths.label: The end standards are two decades apart: divide the potential difference by 2.
A gas probe has a negative slope: use the sign you found in (a).

ecf.label: Consistent with your own slope.
Consistent with your own log c.

paths.label: Undo the dilution by multiplying by V_b/V_a.

variants.stem: For the glass pH electrode: (a) in which solution is it conditioned, and for how long, (b) which surface group forms, and (c) which class of ions interferes?
variants.explanation: Conditioning in 0.1 M HCl for about an hour forms silanol groups (–SiO⁻H⁺) in a thin surface layer. The response is to H⁺ activity; alkali-metal ions (Na⁺, Li⁺, K⁺) interfere, more so as the Al₂O₃ content rises.

variants.stem: For the fluoride ISE: (a) what is the membrane, (b) what is it doped with to raise mobility, and (c) which ion is the main interferent?
variants.explanation: A single crystal of LaF₃ doped with EuF₂; F⁻ hops between vacancies (a defect mechanism). The main interferent is hydroxide, which is why TISAB buffers the pH to 5–6.

variants.stem: A PVC membrane sensor has four components. Name each in order of amount: ~30%, 65–70%, ~1%, and the ~1% that is sometimes added to raise conductivity.
variants.explanation: Polymer (PVC, ~30%); plasticiser (a solvent keeping the polymer liquid-like, 65–70%); ionophore (selective complexing agent, ~1%); salt (conductivity / counter-ion, ~1%).

variants.stem: The fluoride ionic strength adjustment buffer (TISAB) has three components. State the job of (a) NaCl, (b) sodium acetate, (c) CDTA.
variants.explanation: NaCl fixes the ionic strength so γ is constant and the electrode follows concentration. Acetate holds pH at 5–6 so OH⁻ does not interfere. CDTA complexes Al(III) and Fe(III), which would otherwise bind F⁻.

variants.stem: For the PVC potassium electrode: (a) which ionophore is used, (b) why must the electrode be very selective for K⁺ over Na⁺ in serum, and (c) why is an NH₄NO₃ bridge used?
variants.explanation: Valinomycin; its cavity size gives high K⁺ selectivity. Serum K⁺ is 3.5–5.0 mM but Na⁺ is 135–145 mM, so Na⁺ is ~30× more abundant. The NH₄NO₃ bridge stops K⁺ leaking from the saturated KCl reference into the sample.

variants.stem: Compare molecular fluorescence with molecular absorption spectrometry: how the signal is measured, instrument geometry, and sensitivity.
variants.explanation: Absorption measures the light lost through the sample in line with the beam; fluorescence measures light emitted at a longer wavelength, viewed at 90° against a dark background, which makes it more sensitive and more selective (two wavelengths).

rubric.criterion: Absorption: measures the light lost (transmitted vs incident) in line with the beam; signal is a small difference at low concentration
Fluorescence: measures emitted light, at a longer wavelength than the excitation (Stokes shift)
Emission is detected at 90° to the excitation beam so transmitted source light is not seen
Because the signal is measured against a dark background, fluorescence has lower detection limits; two wavelengths (excitation and emission) also improve selectivity

variants.stem: Describe how atomic absorption spectrometry works: the main components and how an absorbance is related to concentration.
variants.explanation: A hollow-cathode lamp of the analyte element emits its narrow lines; the atomiser (flame or furnace) produces free atoms from the sample; the monochromator isolates the line; the detector measures the light lost. A = ε b c holds for the atom cloud, so a calibration of A against concentration gives the sample.

rubric.criterion: Hollow-cathode lamp of the element sought supplies narrow line radiation
Atomiser (flame or graphite furnace) converts the sample into free ground-state atoms
Monochromator isolates the analytical line; detector measures the intensity before and after
Absorbance is proportional to the atom concentration (Beer–Lambert), so a calibration curve gives the unknown

variants.stem: The energy-level diagram of a molecule shows the singlet states S₀ and S₁, each with vibrational levels, and a triplet state T₁ just below S₁. Name the process shown by each arrow.
variants.explanation: Absorption is the upward arrow from S₀. Vibrational relaxation drops the molecule to the lowest vibrational level of S₁ by giving energy to the solvent. Internal conversion is the non-radiative step between electronic states of the same spin (S₁ into a high vibrational level of S₀). Intersystem crossing is the isoenergetic non-radiative step between states of different spin (S₁ to T₁). Fluorescence and phosphorescence are the two photon-emitting steps: S₁ → S₀ (same spin, fast) and T₁ → S₀ (spin change, slow).

fields.label: Upward arrow from the lowest vibrational level of S₀ to a high vibrational level of S₁
Short non-radiative steps down the vibrational levels of S₁ to its lowest level, energy passed to the solvent
Non-radiative step from the lowest level of S₁ into a high vibrational level of S₀ (same spin)
Isoenergetic non-radiative step from S₁ to the triplet state T₁ (spin changes)
Photon emitted in S₁ → S₀ (same spin, lifetime about 10⁻⁹ to 10⁻⁴ s)
Photon emitted in T₁ → S₀ (spin changes, lifetime about 10⁻⁴ to 10² s)

variants.perspectiveLabel: Name processes A to E (5 marks)
variants.stem: In a Jablonski diagram the arrows are lettered. **A** is the upward arrow from S₀; **B** is a downward photon-emitting arrow from the lowest level of S₁ to S₀; **C** is a downward photon-emitting arrow from the lowest level of T₁ to S₀; **D** is a horizontal non-radiative step from S₁ into a high vibrational level of S₀; **E** is a horizontal isoenergetic step from S₁ to T₁. Name each process.
variants.explanation: A = absorption, B = fluorescence (S₁ → S₀, same spin), C = phosphorescence (T₁ → S₀, spin change, slower), D = internal conversion (non-radiative, same spin), E = intersystem crossing (non-radiative, between different multiplicities). The short vibrational relaxation steps (R) are not lettered here.

variants.stem: With reference to the energy-level diagram, explain what happens when a molecule **absorbs radiation but neither fluoresces nor phosphoresces**.
variants.explanation: Absorption lifts the molecule to an upper vibrational level of S₁. Vibrational relaxation (R) takes it to the lowest vibrational level of S₁, passing energy to the solvent. Internal conversion then moves it from S₁ into a high vibrational level of S₀ without any light being emitted, and a second vibrational relaxation brings it to the bottom of S₀. All the energy ends as heat.

rubric.criterion: Absorption raises the molecule from the lowest level of S₀ to an upper vibrational level of S₁
Vibrational relaxation (R) takes it to the lowest vibrational level of S₁, passing energy to the solvent
Internal conversion carries it from S₁ into a high vibrational level of S₀ without emitting light
Vibrational relaxation to the bottom of S₀: the excess energy ends as heat

variants.stem: With reference to the same diagram, explain what happens when a molecule **absorbs radiation and then fluoresces**. Which molecules do this?
variants.explanation: The first steps are the same: absorption to an upper vibrational level of S₁ and vibrational relaxation to the bottom of S₁. Instead of internal conversion, the molecule emits a photon and drops straight to S₀ (a vibrational level of the ground state). This is favoured in rigid molecules, which cannot lose their energy easily through vibration.

rubric.criterion: Absorption to an upper vibrational level of S₁, as before
Vibrational relaxation to the lowest level of S₁
Instead of internal conversion the molecule emits a photon in the transition S₁ → S₀ (fluorescence)
This happens for rigid molecules that do not lose energy easily by vibration

variants.stem: Explain how **molecular fluorescence differs from molecular phosphorescence**.
variants.explanation: Fluorescence is the emission of a photon in a transition between states of the same spin (S₁ → S₀) and is fast, with a lifetime of about 10⁻⁹ to 10⁻⁴ s. For phosphorescence the molecule must first cross from the singlet S₁ to the triplet T₁ by intersystem crossing (an isoenergetic non-radiative step between different multiplicities); the photon is then emitted in the spin-changing transition T₁ → S₀, which is slow, with a lifetime of about 10⁻⁴ to 10² s. (Standard physics, not on the slides: T₁ lies below S₁, so phosphorescence appears at a longer wavelength.)

rubric.criterion: Fluorescence: a photon is emitted in a transition between states of the same spin (S₁ → S₀)
Fluorescence is fast: lifetime about 10⁻⁹ to 10⁻⁴ s
Phosphorescence needs intersystem crossing first: an isoenergetic non-radiative step from the singlet S₁ to the triplet T₁
Phosphorescence: a photon is emitted in a transition between states of different spin (T₁ → S₀)
Phosphorescence is much slower: lifetime about 10⁻⁴ to 10² s
Clear comparison of the two: both are radiative, but they differ in spin change and lifetime

variants.perspectiveLabel: Why fluorescence is more sensitive (4 marks)
variants.stem: Why are **fluorescence measurements more sensitive than absorbance measurements** for solution-phase species?
variants.explanation: Fluorescence is measured against a zero background: the detector sits at 90° to the excitation beam, so only light emitted by the sample reaches it, and a detector can be made very responsive to a small signal on nothing. Absorbance is the small decrease in a large transmitted beam, which means measuring a small difference between two large intensities, and that is hard to do accurately. The effect is like spotting a faint light in a dark room compared with a brightly lit one.

rubric.criterion: Fluorescence is measured against a zero (dark) background
The detector is at right angles to the excitation beam, so only light emitted by the sample reaches it
Absorbance is a small decrease in a large transmitted signal (a small difference between two large intensities), which is hard to measure accurately
So the fluorescence detector can be made far more responsive to small signals (dark-room analogy)

variants.stem: Which kinds of molecule are most likely to fluoresce strongly, and why?
variants.explanation: Rigid molecules, such as polycyclic aromatic compounds, and many substituted aromatics, fluoresce strongly (quantum yield close to 1). They have few ways to lose the excitation energy by vibration, so internal conversion competes poorly with emission. A rise in temperature lowers the quantum yield.

rubric.criterion: Rigid molecules such as polycyclic aromatic compounds (and many substituted aromatics)
They lose less of the excitation energy by vibration and internal conversion, so more excited molecules emit (quantum yield near 1; higher temperature lowers it)

variants.perspectiveLabel: Why absorption bands are broad (2 marks)
variants.stem: Why are molecular absorption bands in solution **broad** rather than sharp lines?
variants.explanation: Each electronic transition has many closely spaced vibrational and rotational levels superimposed on it, and the solvent adds further interaction, so absorption occurs over a wide range of wavelengths instead of at one.

rubric.criterion: Each electronic transition has many closely spaced vibrational and rotational levels superimposed on it
Absorption therefore occurs over a range of wavelengths (solvent interactions add to the broadening)

variants.stem: What is the **Stokes shift**, what causes it, and when are the absorption and emission spectra mirror images?
variants.explanation: The Stokes shift is the displacement of the emission to a longer wavelength than the radiation that excited it. It is caused by re-optimisation of the molecule’s geometry in the excited state S₁ and by interactions with the surrounding solvent, which lose some of the energy before the photon is emitted. The spectra are approximate mirror images when the vibrational spacings are similar in the two states and the transition probabilities are similar; that is a condition on the spectra, not the cause of the shift.

rubric.criterion: Emission occurs at a longer wavelength than the excitation radiation
Cause: re-optimisation of the molecule’s geometry in the excited state S₁
Cause: interactions with the environment (solvent)
The spectra are approximate mirror images when vibrational spacings and transition probabilities are similar (a condition, not the cause)

variants.stem: What is **fluorescence quenching**, and how does the Stern–Volmer relation show it?
variants.explanation: Quenching happens when the energy of the excited molecule is transferred to another molecule, the quencher Q, instead of being emitted: M* + Q → M + Q*, after which Q* loses its energy as heat. The booklet gives Φ₀/Φ_Q = 1 + (k_q/(k_e + k_d))[Q], so the ratio of the fluorescence quantum yield without and with quencher rises linearly with the quencher concentration.

rubric.criterion: Quenching: the excited molecule transfers its energy to another molecule (the quencher Q) instead of emitting
M* + Q → M + Q*, then Q* → Q + heat
Stern–Volmer: Φ₀/Φ_Q = 1 + (k_q/(k_e + k_d))[Q], a straight line against [Q]

variants.explanation: Source → wavelength selection for the excitation (a monochromator or filter; not needed for a line source such as a hollow-cathode lamp) → sample cell → emission monochromator and photomultiplier detector placed at 90° to the excitation beam → readout. variants.stem: Describe the **hollow-cathode lamp** used in atomic absorption spectroscopy: what it is made of, how it works and what it emits.
variants.explanation: The cathode is made of the metal being determined and the lamp is filled with argon. A high voltage ionises the argon to Ar⁺ and electrons; Ar⁺ strikes the cathode and dislodges metal atoms (sputtering); the sputtered atoms collide with energetic electrons and are excited. The excited atoms emit lines of exactly the frequency the analyte absorbs, and these lines are narrower than about 10⁻³ to 10⁻² nm.

rubric.criterion: Cathode made of the metal being determined; lamp filled with argon
High voltage ionises Ar to Ar⁺ and e⁻; Ar⁺ sputters metal atoms off the cathode and they are excited by collisions with energetic electrons
The excited atoms emit the analyte’s own lines (same frequency the analyte absorbs), narrower than about 10⁻³ to 10⁻² nm

variants.stem: Describe the **atomiser (flame)** in atomic absorption spectroscopy: how the sample reaches it and what happens there.
variants.explanation: The nebuliser turns the sample solution into a fine aerosol that mixes with fuel and oxidant; baffles remove large droplets, so only about 5% of the sample reaches the flame. The solvent burns off (desolvation in the primary combustion zone), then the particles vaporise and are atomised, mainly in the hot interzonal region, giving free ground-state atoms that absorb the lamp radiation. Oxides and hydroxides form in the outer cone, so the hottest region is wanted.

rubric.criterion: The nebuliser makes a fine aerosol that mixes with fuel and oxidant (baffles remove large drops; only about 5% reaches the flame)
The solvent burns off, then the particles vaporise and are atomised, in the hottest (interzonal) region, to avoid oxide formation
The result is free ground-state atoms that absorb the radiation from the lamp

variants.stem: What is the **monochromator** for in an atomic absorption spectrometer, and how does slit width matter?
variants.explanation: It isolates the analytical line from the lamp (and from light emitted by the flame and other lines) using an entrance slit, a grating and an exit slit. Slit width trades resolution against light throughput: a narrow slit separates neighbouring lines better but passes less light; a wide slit passes more light but resolves less. (Several past keys say the opposite, that a wider slit gives higher resolution; the lecture and the physics agree with the trade-off written here.)

rubric.criterion: Isolates the analytical line from the lamp, and from flame emission and other lines (entrance slit, grating, exit slit)
Slit width trades resolution against light throughput (signal)

variants.stem: Describe the **detector** (photomultiplier) used in atomic absorption spectroscopy.
variants.explanation: A photomultiplier converts photons into electrons. Each photon striking the photoemissive cathode ejects electrons, which are focused onto a dynode that releases more electrons, and this is repeated several times, so one photon gives about a million electrons (the key’s figure). The resulting current is amplified and read out.

rubric.criterion: Photons strike a photoemissive cathode and eject electrons
The electrons are multiplied at successive dynodes (about 10⁶ electrons per photon in the key); the amplified current is read out

variants.explanation: Hollow-cathode lamp: cathode of the analyte metal, argon fill, high voltage, Ar⁺ sputters metal atoms that are excited and emit the analyte lines (narrower than 10⁻³–10⁻² nm). Flame: nebuliser makes an aerosol, fuel and oxidant, desolvation, vaporisation and atomisation in the hot region, free ground-state atoms absorb. Monochromator: slits and grating isolate the line; slit width trades resolution against throughput. Detector: photomultiplier with dynode multiplication, amplified signal.

metadata.title: Boltzmann populations: why emission is temperature-sensitive

variants.stem: The lowest excited state of sodium is **3.371 × 10⁻¹⁹ J** above the ground state and the excited state has degeneracy 2 (ground state 1); *k* = 1.381 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹. Calculate the **percentage of Na atoms in the excited state** at **{{fix(T1,0)}} K** and at **{{fix(T2,0)}} K**, and the **percentage increase** in the excited-state population between the two temperatures.
variants.hint: N_e/N₀ = 2 exp[−ΔE/(kT)]. Percentage = 100 × that ratio.
variants.explanation: N_e/N₀ = (g_e/g₀) exp[−(E_e − E₀)/kT]. Multiply by 100 for a percentage. Only a tiny fraction of the atoms (well under 0.1%) is ever excited, so almost all atoms stay in the ground state whatever the temperature; but the excited population changes by a large percentage for a small change in temperature. That is why emission (which depends on the excited population) is far more temperature-sensitive than absorption (which depends on the ground-state atoms).

ecf.label: Consistent with your own two percentages.

metadata.title: AES vs AAS: temperature, types, no Stokes shift

variants.perspectiveLabel: AES vs AAS temperature sensitivity (5 marks)
variants.stem: Explain why **atomic emission spectroscopy is more sensitive to fluctuations in flame temperature than atomic absorption spectroscopy**. Use the Boltzmann distribution.
variants.explanation: N_e/N₀ = (g_e/g₀) exp[−(E_e − E₀)/kT]. For sodium at 2500 K only about 1×10⁻⁴ of the atoms are excited, so more than 99.98% are in the ground state. A small rise in temperature (for example 20 K) changes that tiny excited population by a large percentage (about 8%) but hardly changes the ground-state population. Emission is proportional to the excited-state population, so it responds strongly; absorption is by the ground-state atoms, which hardly change, so it is much less sensitive.

rubric.criterion: States the Boltzmann relation N_e/N₀ = (g_e/g₀) exp[−(E_e − E₀)/kT]
Only a tiny fraction of the atoms is excited (for example about 10⁻⁴ for Na near 2500 K), so almost all atoms are in the ground state
A small temperature change alters that tiny excited population by a large percentage (for example about 8% for 20 K)
Emission depends on the excited-state population, so it is very temperature-sensitive
Absorption depends on the ground-state atoms, whose number hardly changes, so AAS is much less sensitive

variants.stem: In which kind of atomic spectroscopy is the signal **emission from an excited state populated thermally**, without any lamp?
variants.explanation: **Atomic emission spectroscopy (AES)**, for example ICP-OES: a hot plasma excites the atoms thermally and the emitted light is measured. In AAS sharp lamp lines are absorbed by ground-state atoms; in atomic fluorescence the emission follows an initial absorption of radiation.

variants.stem: Why does atomic emission show no Stokes shift (the emission wavelength equals the excitation wavelength)?
variants.explanation: Atoms have no molecular orbitals, vibrations or geometry to re-optimise, so no energy is lost between excitation and emission. The Stokes shift belongs to molecular fluorescence.

options.label: there are no molecular orbitals, so no vibrational relaxation or re-optimisation takes place
because atomic lines are broader than molecular bands
because the plasma is cooler than a flame
because atoms emit only in the infrared

variants.stem: Describe the processes that lead to **broadening of atomic linewidths**.
variants.explanation: Natural broadening comes from the Heisenberg uncertainty principle, δE δt ≥ h/4π: an excited state with a short lifetime (about 10⁻⁸ to 10⁻⁹ s) has an uncertain energy, giving widths of about 10⁻⁵ to 10⁻⁴ nm. Collisional (pressure) broadening: collisions between atoms shorten the lifetime of the excited state, and it grows with temperature (up to about 10⁻³ nm for Na). Doppler broadening: atoms moving toward the detector emit light seen at a higher frequency and atoms moving away at a lower frequency, and the spread of velocities broadens the line; it grows with temperature.

rubric.criterion: Natural broadening: Heisenberg uncertainty, a short excited-state lifetime gives an uncertain energy (δE δt ≥ h/4π)
Collisional (pressure) broadening: collisions between atoms shorten the excited-state lifetime
Doppler broadening: atoms moving toward or away from the detector shift the observed frequency up or down; the spread of velocities broadens the line
Collisional and Doppler broadening increase with temperature
Typical widths: natural about 10⁻⁵–10⁻⁴ nm; collisional up to about 10⁻³ nm

variants.perspectiveLabel: Why lamp lines are narrower than flame lines (2 marks)
variants.stem: Why are the lines emitted by a **hollow-cathode lamp narrower** than the absorption lines of atoms in a flame, and why does that matter for AAS?
variants.explanation: The gas in the lamp is cooler and at lower pressure than the flame, so there is less Doppler and pressure broadening. A monochromator cannot isolate lines narrower than about 10⁻³ to 10⁻² nm, so a line source whose lines are narrower than the absorption lines is needed for Beer’s law to hold.

rubric.criterion: The lamp is cooler and at lower pressure than the flame, so there is less Doppler and pressure broadening
A monochromator cannot isolate such narrow lines (below about 10⁻³–10⁻² nm), so AAS needs a line source

variants.perspectiveLabel: Molecular bands vs atomic lines (4 marks)
variants.stem: Why are **molecular emission bands much broader than atomic emission lines**, and what controls the width of atomic lines?
variants.explanation: In molecules the electronic transitions have vibrational and rotational levels superimposed on them, so each transition spreads into a band. In atoms only electronic levels are involved, so the lines are narrow. Their widths are set by natural broadening (the Heisenberg uncertainty principle), collisional (pressure) broadening and Doppler broadening, the last two growing with temperature.

rubric.criterion: Molecular transitions include vibrational and rotational levels superimposed on the electronic change, so they spread into bands
Atomic transitions are electronic only, so the lines are narrow
Atomic widths are controlled by natural (Heisenberg) broadening
and by collisional (pressure) and Doppler broadening, which grow with temperature

variants.stem: Outline the **advantages of inductively coupled plasma – optical emission spectroscopy (ICP-OES) compared with AAS**.
variants.explanation: ICP-OES measures many elements at once (a polychromator with many exit slits and detectors) without changing a lamp for each element. The argon plasma is much hotter (6,000 to 10,000 K, fairly uniform across its cross-section), so desolvation, vaporisation and atomisation are essentially complete and a good excited-state population is reached. The inert argon atmosphere also means fewer oxides form.

rubric.criterion: Many elements measured simultaneously, without a separate lamp for each element
Much hotter plasma (6,000–10,000 K): more complete atomisation and excitation
Inert argon atmosphere, so less oxide formation

variants.perspectiveLabel: Molecular vs atomic method for lead (4 marks)
variants.stem: Lead can be determined by UV-vis spectroscopy after complexing Pb²⁺ with a ligand, or by atomic absorption or emission. Give **one advantage of each approach** (two points each).
variants.explanation: Molecular (complexation and UV-vis): it measures only free Pb²⁺, which is what you want if speciation matters, and it needs no flame or high temperature, which is cheaper and safer. Atomic methods: they measure all forms of lead at once (total lead), and because only a very narrow wavelength is measured there are fewer interferences.

rubric.criterion: Molecular: measures only the free Pb²⁺ (useful when speciation matters)
Molecular: no flame or high temperature needed (cheaper, safer)
Atomic: measures all forms of lead, so gives the total lead
Atomic: only a very narrow wavelength is measured, so fewer interferences

variants.stem: How must **PM2.5 samples be prepared** before elemental analysis by atomic spectroscopy?
variants.explanation: The particles are collected on filter paper. The filter is digested by microwave-assisted acid digestion so that the particulate matter dissolves completely, and the solution is then analysed by ICP spectroscopy.

rubric.criterion: Collect the particles on a filter, then dissolve them completely by microwave-assisted acid digestion
Analyse the resulting solution by ICP spectroscopy (ICP-OES or ICP-MS)

metadata.title: GC detectors: TCD, FID and MS
metadata.source: GC and HPLC slides; final Q4 style

variants.stem: Describe the principle of the **thermal conductivity detector (TCD)** used in gas chromatography.
variants.explanation: A heated filament sits in the gas leaving the column. Helium carries heat away from it at a steady rate. When an analyte elutes, the thermal conductivity of the gas changes, so the filament temperature and resistance change (a Wheatstone bridge goes out of balance) and that is the signal. The TCD responds to almost any compound, does not destroy the sample, and is less sensitive than the FID.

rubric.criterion: A heated filament sits in the gas leaving the column; the carrier gas (usually helium, a good heat conductor) carries heat away at a steady rate
When an analyte elutes, the thermal conductivity of the gas changes, so the filament temperature and resistance change (Wheatstone bridge unbalanced) and this is the signal
Near-universal and non-destructive, but less sensitive than the FID

variants.stem: Describe the principle of the **flame ionisation detector (FID)** used in gas chromatography.
variants.explanation: The column effluent is burned in a hydrogen–air flame. Organic compounds form ions in the flame, and the resulting ion current is the signal. The FID is very sensitive to organic compounds (including the small samples from capillary columns) but it destroys the sample.

rubric.criterion: The column effluent is burned in a hydrogen–air flame
Organic compounds form ions in the flame and the resulting ion current is measured as the signal
Highly sensitive to organic compounds (suits the small samples of capillary columns) but destructive

variants.perspectiveLabel: Mass spectrometer as a detector (3 marks)
variants.stem: Explain how a **mass spectrometer** works as a GC detector and what it adds compared with the TCD and FID.
variants.explanation: Molecules from the sample are converted into ions; the ions are separated in the mass analyser by their mass-to-charge ratio (m/z); the detector records each ion signal and the result is a mass spectrum. Unlike the TCD and FID, which only say that something eluted, the spectrum identifies each compound.

rubric.criterion: Sample molecules are first converted into ions
The ions are separated in the mass analyser according to their mass-to-charge ratio (m/z)
The signals form a mass spectrum, giving specific identification of each compound (TCD and FID only show that something eluted)

variants.stem: One GC analysis must detect **trace hydrocarbons**; another must detect **permanent gases and water** that give no response in a flame. Which detector would you use for each, and why?
variants.explanation: Trace hydrocarbons: the FID, because it is highly sensitive to organic compounds; destroying the sample does not matter for a trace determination. Permanent gases and water: the TCD, because it responds to almost anything whose thermal conductivity differs from the carrier gas (helium), and it does not destroy the sample, although it is less sensitive.

rubric.criterion: Trace hydrocarbons: FID
Reason: highly sensitive to organic compounds (ions formed in the flame); destroying the sample is acceptable
Permanent gases and water: TCD
Reason: near-universal response to anything whose thermal conductivity differs from the carrier gas (helium); non-destructive but less sensitive

metadata.title: GC columns: open tubular and packed
metadata.source: GC and HPLC slides; final Q4 style

variants.stem: Compare **open tubular (capillary)** and **packed** GC columns in construction and performance, and give **two applications** for which capillary columns are preferred.
variants.explanation: An open tubular column is a narrow tube with the stationary phase coated on its inner wall and nothing packed inside. A packed column is filled with particles of support coated with liquid phase (or the solid is the phase). Open tubular columns give higher resolution, shorter analysis times and higher sensitivity but hold less sample; packed columns hold more sample but give broader peaks, longer retention and lower resolution. Capillary columns are preferred for complex mixtures that need high resolution and for trace analysis (including GC–MS).

rubric.criterion: Open tubular: narrow tube with the stationary phase on the inner wall, nothing packed inside
Packed: tube filled with particles of coated support (or the solid itself is the stationary phase)
Open tubular: higher resolution, shorter analysis time and higher sensitivity, but lower sample capacity
Packed: higher sample capacity, but broader peaks, longer retention times and lower resolution
Two applications for capillary columns, for example complex mixtures needing high resolution, and trace analysis (including GC–MS)

variants.perspectiveLabel: Kinds of open tubular column (3 marks)
variants.stem: Name the **three kinds of open tubular column** and say what is on the wall of each.
variants.explanation: WCOT (wall-coated): a thin film of liquid stationary phase on the inner wall. PLOT (porous layer): a layer of solid particles that is itself the active phase, used for gases so volatile that a liquid film retains them poorly, such as O₂, N₂ and CO. SCOT (support-coated): solid support particles coated with liquid phase and attached to the wall; it holds more sample than WCOT and performs between WCOT and PLOT.

rubric.criterion: WCOT: a thin film of liquid stationary phase on the inner wall
PLOT: a porous layer of solid particles is the active phase (for very volatile gases such as O₂, N₂, CO)
SCOT: solid support coated with liquid phase attached to the wall; larger sample than WCOT, performance between WCOT and PLOT

variants.stem: Why does band spreading by **multiple paths** (the A term of the van Deemter equation) not occur in an open tubular column, and what does that do to efficiency and flow?
variants.explanation: There are no packed particles, so every molecule follows essentially the same single path along the open tube and the multiple-path term is about zero. Plate height is therefore lower (efficiency higher), and for the same length and pressure the linear flow rate is much higher than in a packed column.

rubric.criterion: No packing, so there is a single open flow path and the multiple-path (eddy diffusion) term A is essentially zero
So plate height is lower (efficiency higher), and the linear flow for the same length and pressure is much higher than in a packed column

metadata.title: Temperature and pressure programming
metadata.source: GC and HPLC slides; final Q4 style

variants.stem: How does **column temperature programming** affect the separation in gas chromatography?
variants.explanation: A sample with a wide boiling range cannot be separated well at one temperature: if the oven is cool the heavy compounds are held too long and give broad peaks, and if it is hot the light compounds all leave together. The program starts low to separate the volatile compounds, then raises the temperature (about 5–20 °C/min) so the less volatile compounds gain vapour pressure and elute sooner, and ends with a hold to clean the column. All compounds elute with adequate resolution in a shorter run and the late peaks are sharper.

rubric.criterion: Problem: a wide boiling range cannot be run well isothermally (cool: heavy compounds retained too long, broad peaks; hot: volatiles bunch together)
Start low to separate the volatile compounds, then raise the temperature so less volatile compounds gain vapour pressure and elute sooner
Result: every compound elutes with adequate resolution in a shorter run, with sharper late peaks (better sensitivity)

variants.stem: Give **two advantages** and **two disadvantages** of temperature programming, and name an alternative that avoids high temperatures.
variants.explanation: Advantages: compounds with very different boiling points all elute with resolution in a reasonable time, and later peaks are sharper so sensitivity improves (a low starting temperature also focuses the band in splitless or on-column injection). Disadvantages: the baseline can slope because the stationary phase bleeds at high temperature, and the oven needs time to cool between runs. Alternative: pressure programming raises the flow instead, shortening the retention of late peaks without high temperature and so sparing thermally sensitive compounds; it needs a costly high-pressure system.

rubric.criterion: Advantage: compounds with very different boiling points all elute with resolution in a reasonable time
Advantage: later peaks are sharper, so sensitivity improves (a low start also focuses the band for splitless or on-column injection)
Disadvantages: sloping baseline from stationary-phase bleed at high temperature; time needed to cool the oven between runs
Alternative: pressure programming (higher flow shortens retention of late peaks without heat, sparing thermally sensitive compounds; costly high-pressure pump)

metadata.title: GC injection modes and derivatisation
metadata.source: GC and HPLC slides; final Q4 style

variants.stem: A sample is so concentrated that the column would be overloaded. Which injection mode is used?
variants.explanation: **Split** injection sends only a small fraction of the vaporised sample onto the column and vents the rest, which avoids overload and keeps the peaks sharp.

options.label: none: the sample must be diluted by 100 times first

variants.stem: A trace-level analyte must reach the column with as little loss as possible. Which injection mode is used?
variants.explanation: **Splitless** injection keeps the split vent closed at first so nearly all the vaporised sample enters the column, then opens it to flush out the remaining solvent vapour. That maximises sensitivity for trace analytes.

options.label: split injection with a high split ratio
split injection at the lowest temperature

variants.stem: A thermally labile, high-boiling compound would decompose in a hot injector. Which injection mode suits it?
variants.explanation: **On-column** injection puts the liquid sample directly onto the cool column, which concentrates the analytes near the entrance; heating the column then starts the separation. Thermal degradation and sample loss are minimal.

variants.stem: A carboxylic acid is not volatile enough for GC. What is the standard remedy?
variants.explanation: **Derivatisation** converts the analyte into a form that is more volatile or easier to detect. A carboxylic acid is converted into its trimethylsilyl ester, which is volatile.

options.label: convert it into a volatile derivative such as the trimethylsilyl ester
switch the carrier gas to nitrogen

metadata.title: GC carrier gases
metadata.source: GC and HPLC slides; final Q4 style

variants.stem: Arranged from lowest to highest optimum flow rate, the usual GC carrier gases are:
variants.explanation: The optimum flow rate rises in the order N₂ < He < H₂, so He and H₂ allow faster analyses than N₂ at the same efficiency.

options.label: all three have the same optimum

variants.stem: Which statement about hydrogen as a carrier gas matches the updated lecture slides?
variants.explanation: Hydrogen has a particularly broad, flat van Deemter optimum, so efficient operation at higher linear velocity gives faster analysis. Its drawbacks are that it is flammable and explosive, and GC–MS use needs a compatible instrument and precautions. (The older slide said it simply cannot be used with MS; use the updated wording.)

options.label: broad flat optimum and faster analysis, but flammable; GC–MS needs a compatible instrument
the slowest of the three carriers
inert, non-flammable and ideal for every detector
it cannot be used with an FID

variants.stem: Which carrier gas is normally used with a TCD, and why?
variants.explanation: Helium: its high thermal conductivity gives a large contrast with most analytes, so an eluting compound changes the thermal conductivity of the gas leaving the column and the filament temperature clearly.

options.label: helium, because of its high thermal conductivity
nitrogen, because it is the cheapest
air, because it supports the flame

metadata.title: HPLC columns: reading the label
metadata.source: GC and HPLC slides; final Q4 style

variants.stem: An HPLC column is labelled **C18, 60 Å, 4 µm, 3.9 × 150 mm**. In the updated lecture, “3.9 × 150 mm” gives:
variants.explanation: Inner diameter × length: the column is 150 mm long with an inner diameter of 3.9 mm. C18 is the bonded stationary phase, 60 Å the pore size and 4 µm the particle size.

options.label: particle size 3.9 µm and pore size 150 Å

variants.stem: Which pore size is chosen for peptides and proteins, compared with small molecules?
variants.explanation: Small molecules use pores of about 100 Å; peptides and proteins are larger and need pores of about 300 Å so that they can enter.

options.label: about 300 Å for peptides and proteins, about 100 Å for small molecules
about 100 Å for peptides and proteins, about 300 Å for small molecules
the same pore size for both
no pores: peptides need non-porous glass

variants.stem: Replacing a C18 column by a C8 column, with the same mobile phase, will usually give:
variants.explanation: C8 has shorter (8-carbon) chains, so the stationary phase is less hydrophobic, hydrophobic analytes stick less and retention is generally shorter.

options.label: shorter retention, because C8 is less hydrophobic
longer retention, because C8 is more polar and more selective

variants.stem: What is a guard column for?
variants.explanation: It protects the analytical column from particulate matter and contaminants in the sample and solvents. It has the same packing and stationary phase, but is shorter and cheaper, so it is the part that gets replaced.

options.label: to protect the analytical column: same packing, shorter and cheaper
to raise the number of plates

variants.stem: What limits the use of silica-based HPLC columns?
variants.explanation: Silica has limited stability at high pH, so other support materials are used when a wider pH range is needed.

options.label: silica is unstable at high pH
silica cannot be bonded to alkyl chains

metadata.title: Normal and reversed phase, eluent strength
metadata.source: GC and HPLC slides; final Q4 style

variants.stem: An HPLC column has a **polar** stationary phase (amino or diol groups) and a **non-polar** mobile phase. Which mode is this and which solutes elute first?
variants.explanation: This is **normal-phase** chromatography. In normal phase the least polar component elutes first, and making the mobile phase more polar increases eluent strength, so solutes elute sooner.

options.label: normal phase; the least polar elutes first
reversed phase; the most polar elutes first
normal phase; the most polar elutes first
reversed phase; the least polar elutes first

variants.stem: On a C18 column with an aqueous–organic mobile phase, which kind of solute elutes first?
variants.explanation: Reversed phase has a non-polar stationary phase and a polar mobile phase. The most polar solute interacts least with the C18 chains and spends most of its time in the mobile phase, so it elutes first. Retention rises with hydrophobicity.

options.label: the largest solute whatever its polarity
the solute present at the highest concentration

variants.stem: In reversed-phase HPLC the percentage of organic solvent (%B, for example acetonitrile) is increased. What happens?
variants.explanation: The mobile phase becomes less polar, so its eluent strength rises. Analytes spend less time on the hydrophobic C18 surface and elute sooner, so retention times fall.

options.label: the eluent is stronger and retention times fall
the eluent is weaker and retention times rise

metadata.title: Elution order in HPLC
metadata.source: GC and HPLC slides; final Q4 style

variants.stem: Put these compounds in the order they elute from a **reversed-phase (C18)** HPLC column: toluene, phenol, butanol, cyclohexane.
variants.explanation: In reversed phase retention rises with hydrophobicity, so the most polar compound leaves first: **butanol → phenol → toluene → cyclohexane**. Butanol and phenol carry an –OH group, toluene is an aromatic hydrocarbon, and cyclohexane is a saturated hydrocarbon with no polar group.

variants.stem: Put these alcohols in the order they elute from a **reversed-phase (C18)** column: 1-butanol, ethanol, 1-pentanol, 1-propanol.
variants.explanation: All four have the same –OH group, so the difference is the length of the hydrocarbon chain. A longer chain is more hydrophobic and interacts more with C18, so retention rises: **ethanol → 1-propanol → 1-butanol → 1-pentanol**.

variants.stem: Put these ethyl halides in the order they elute from a **reversed-phase (C18)** column: C₂H₅Br, C₂H₅F, C₂H₅I, C₂H₅Cl.
variants.explanation: Hydrophobicity increases down the halogen series F < Cl < Br < I, so interaction with C18 and retention increase in the same order: **C₂H₅F → C₂H₅Cl → C₂H₅Br → C₂H₅I**.

variants.stem: Put these in the order they elute from a **reversed-phase (C18)** column: toluene, hexadecane, methanol, acetone.
variants.explanation: The –OH group makes methanol very polar, the C=O group of acetone is polar but less hydrophilic, toluene has only C and H (an aromatic hydrocarbon), and hexadecane has a long hydrocarbon chain and is the most hydrophobic: **methanol → acetone → toluene → hexadecane**.

variants.stem: Put these alcohols in the order they elute from a **normal-phase (polar silica-type)** column: ethanol, 1-pentanol, 1-propanol, 1-butanol.
variants.explanation: In normal phase the least polar component elutes first. A longer hydrocarbon chain makes the alcohol less polar, so the order is the reverse of reversed phase: **1-pentanol → 1-butanol → 1-propanol → ethanol**.

variants.stem: Put these in the order they elute from a **normal-phase (polar silica-type)** column: acetone, methanol, hexadecane, toluene.
variants.explanation: In normal phase the least polar compound elutes first, so the order is the reverse of reversed phase: **hexadecane → toluene → acetone → methanol**.

metadata.title: Isocratic and gradient elution
metadata.source: GC and HPLC slides; final Q4 style

variants.stem: Explain the difference between **isocratic** and **gradient** elution in HPLC, and give one advantage of gradient elution.
variants.explanation: In isocratic elution the mobile-phase composition stays constant. In gradient elution the composition changes during the run, continuously or in steps; in reversed phase this means more organic solvent as the run proceeds, which raises the eluent strength. The advantage is that strongly retained compounds elute sooner, so the run is shorter and late peaks are sharper, and one run copes with a sample that contains both weakly and strongly retained compounds.

rubric.criterion: Isocratic: the mobile-phase composition is constant throughout the run
Gradient: the composition is changed during the run, continuously or stepwise (in reversed phase, more organic solvent with time)
Advantage: strongly retained compounds elute sooner, giving a shorter run
Late peaks are sharper, so one run copes with a mixture of weakly and strongly retained solutes

variants.stem: A sample contains both weakly and strongly retained compounds. A single constant solvent composition would either leave the early peaks unresolved or take very long to elute the last ones. What is the usual solution?
variants.explanation: **Gradient elution**: start with a weaker mobile phase to resolve the early peaks, then increase the eluent strength so the strongly retained compounds leave in reasonable time.

options.label: switch from HPLC to a TCD

variants.stem: In a reversed-phase gradient, mobile phase A is water and B is acetonitrile. As the run proceeds %B rises. Which statement is correct?
variants.explanation: Raising %B makes the mobile phase less polar, so the eluent strength increases and retained hydrophobic compounds elute sooner.

options.label: the mobile phase becomes less polar and a stronger eluent
the mobile phase becomes more polar and a stronger eluent
the eluent strength falls, so retention increases
the stationary phase changes to normal phase

metadata.title: HPLC detectors
metadata.source: GC and HPLC slides; final Q4 style

variants.stem: Which is the most common HPLC detector?
variants.explanation: The **UV (spectroscopic) detector**, with a lamp and a monochromator or a photodiode array. It is linear over about five orders of magnitude of solute concentration.

variants.stem: Which HPLC detector responds to almost any solute but is much less sensitive than UV?
variants.explanation: The **refractive index detector** is universal, but its detection limit is far poorer than that of the UV detector (the slides say by about a factor of 1000).

variants.stem: Which HPLC detector is highly selective and sensitive but only responds to electroactive compounds?
variants.explanation: The **electrochemical detector**: only compounds that can be oxidised or reduced at the electrode respond, which makes it selective as well as sensitive.

metadata.title: Why HPLC columns use small packed particles
metadata.source: GC and HPLC slides; final Q4 style

variants.stem: Why do HPLC columns use **small, uniformly packed particles**, and what is the cost?
variants.explanation: Diffusion in liquids is slow, so long diffusion paths cause band broadening. Small particles shorten the distances molecules must diffuse (smaller mass-transfer C term) and pack more uniformly (smaller multiple-path A term). Efficiency rises, N ∝ L/dₚ, so resolution improves or the run can be faster at the same resolution. The cost is that the narrow gaps between small particles resist flow, so a higher pressure is needed.

rubric.criterion: Liquid diffusion is slow, so small particles shorten the diffusion paths and reduce mass-transfer broadening (smaller C term)
More uniform packing reduces multiple-path broadening (smaller A term); efficiency rises (N ∝ L/dₚ), so resolution improves
Cost: smaller particles resist flow, so a higher pressure is needed

metadata.title: Coupling to mass spectrometry: GC–MS and LC–MS
metadata.source: GC and HPLC slides; final Q4 style

variants.stem: Why is **GC–MS** generally easier to interface than **LC–MS**? Describe **two** technical challenges of coupling LC to MS.
variants.explanation: The GC effluent is already a gas and is compatible with the vacuum of the mass spectrometer. The LC effluent is a liquid, so (1) it must be converted into gas-phase ions by an interface such as electrospray (ESI) or atmospheric-pressure chemical ionisation (APCI); (2) the large amount of solvent must be removed (desolvation) before the ions reach the high vacuum; and (3) the mobile phase must be MS-compatible, because non-volatile salts and buffers contaminate the source and suppress ionisation.

rubric.criterion: GC: the effluent is already a gas and is compatible with the MS vacuum
LC challenge 1: the liquid effluent must be converted into gas-phase ions, using an interface such as ESI or APCI
LC challenge 2: the large solvent load must be removed (desolvated) before the ions enter the high vacuum
Further LC point: the mobile phase must be MS-compatible (volatile buffers); non-volatile salts contaminate the source and suppress ionisation
Clear statement of why this makes GC–MS easier (no solvent removal or ion-generation interface needed)

variants.stem: Which kinds of analyte suit **HPLC** rather than GC, and why does that make LC–MS attractive?
variants.explanation: HPLC suits polar, non-volatile and thermally labile compounds, which cannot be vaporised without decomposing. Soft ionisation such as electrospray makes gas-phase ions from these compounds without needing to vaporise them by heat, so LC–MS can analyse compounds that GC–MS cannot.

rubric.criterion: HPLC suits polar, non-volatile or thermally labile analytes (they cannot be vaporised without decomposing)
Electrospray-type interfaces give gas-phase ions without heating the analyte to vaporise it, so LC–MS reaches compounds GC–MS cannot

metadata.title: GC or HPLC?
metadata.source: GC and HPLC slides; final Q4 style

variants.explanation: **GC**: the analytes are volatile and thermally stable, which is exactly what GC needs (gas or volatile liquid stable at roughly 50–300 °C). An FID would detect them sensitively.

variants.stem: You must analyse a thermally labile, non-volatile peptide. Which technique is the natural choice?
variants.explanation: **HPLC** (and LC–MS with electrospray if identification is needed): the peptide would decompose long before it vaporised in a GC oven.

variants.stem: A polar, non-volatile drug must be separated from its metabolites in a urine extract. Which technique is the natural choice?
variants.explanation: **Reversed-phase HPLC**: the polar, non-volatile analytes cannot be vaporised for GC without derivatisation, and reversed phase handles polar compounds well (most polar elutes first).

variants.stem:
A solute dissolved in **{{fix(Vaq,0)}} mL of water** is extracted with an organic solvent. Its partition coefficient is **K = {{fix(K,0)}}** (K = c_org/c_aq).

(a) What percentage of the solute stays in the water after **one** extraction with **{{fix(Vtot,0)}} mL** of solvent?
(b) What percentage stays after **{{fix(ns,0)}} extractions** with {{fix(Ve,1)}} mL each (the same total volume)?
(c) How many extractions with {{fix(Ve,1)}} mL portions are needed to leave no more than **{{fix(x,1)}}%** in the water?
(d) Which way removes more solute?
variants.hint: The solute starts in the water: after one extraction f = V_aq/(V_aq + K V_org). After n extractions the fraction is fⁿ. n = ln(target)/ln f for one portion size, rounded up.
variants.explanation: f = V_aq/(V_aq + K V_org) for each extraction when the solute starts in the water. One extraction with the whole volume leaves f₁; n portions of V_org/n leave (V_aq/(V_aq + K V_org/n))ⁿ, which is smaller: several small extractions beat one large one because each re-applies the equilibrium to what is left. The number needed is n = ln(target)/ln(f per portion), rounded up.

variants.perspectiveLabel: Which pH leaves more acid in the ether (4 marks)
variants.stem: Benzoic acid (a weak acid) in diethyl ether is extracted with an aqueous solution. Would you expect the concentration of benzoic acid left in the ether to be **higher after extraction at pH 5 or at pH 9**? Explain your reasoning.
variants.explanation: The neutral acid HA prefers the organic phase; its anion A⁻ stays in the water. At pH 9, well above the pKa (about 4.2), the acid is almost completely ionised, so the distribution coefficient D = K/(1 + K_a/[H⁺]) is tiny and almost all of the acid moves into the water. At pH 5, close to the pKa, a good fraction is still un-ionised, D is larger and more acid remains in the ether. So the ether holds more acid after extraction at pH 5.

rubric.criterion: The neutral acid HA prefers the organic phase; the ionised form A⁻ stays in the water
At pH 9 (well above the pKa) the acid is mostly ionised, so D is very small and nearly all of it moves into the water
At pH 5 (near the pKa) much of the acid is still un-ionised, so D is larger and more stays in the ether
So the ether concentration is higher after extraction at pH 5 (supported by D = K/(1 + K_a/[H⁺]))

variants.perspectiveLabel: Why several small extractions win (3 marks)
variants.stem: With the same total volume of solvent, why do **several small extractions** remove more solute than **one large extraction**?
variants.explanation: Each extraction re-applies the partition equilibrium to the solute that is still left. After n portions of V_org/n the fraction left in the water is [V_aq/(V_aq + K V_org/n)]ⁿ, which is smaller than V_aq/(V_aq + K V_org) for one large portion. The gain levels off as n grows, so a few portions capture most of the benefit.

rubric.criterion: Each extraction re-applies the equilibrium to the solute still left, starting again from a smaller amount
The fraction left after n portions, [V_aq/(V_aq + K V_org/n)]ⁿ, is smaller than for one portion V_org
So the same total volume extracts more when split (with diminishing returns as n grows)

variants.stem: What is the difference between the **partition coefficient K** and the **distribution coefficient D**, and when are they equal?
variants.explanation: K describes the equilibrium of one chemical form (the neutral molecule) between the two solvents and does not change with pH. D is the overall ratio of the total concentration in the organic phase to the total concentration (all forms, such as HA and A⁻, or B and BH⁺) in the aqueous phase, so it depends on pH. They are equal when the solute exists in only one form, for example an acid at low pH or a base at high pH, where D approaches K.

rubric.criterion: K: ratio of the concentration of the neutral species in the two phases; it does not depend on pH
D: ratio of the total concentration in the organic phase to the total in the aqueous phase (all forms, such as HA and A⁻); it depends on pH
They are equal when the solute is present in one form only (an acid at low pH, a base at high pH), where D approaches K

variants.stem: A solute starts in **50 mL of organic solvent** and is shaken once with **25 mL of water**. Its distribution coefficient is D = 2 (organic/aqueous). Which expression gives the fraction left in the organic phase?
variants.explanation: The solute starts in the organic phase, so f = V_org/(V_org + V_aq/D) = 50/(50 + 25/2). The expression 25/(25 + 2 × 50) is the one for a solute that starts in the water.

variants.perspectiveLabel: Lowering the pH for a base
variants.stem: The pH of the aqueous phase is lowered while a weak base B is extracted. Which statement is correct?
variants.explanation: Lower pH converts more of B into BH⁺, which is ionic and stays in the water, so D falls and more of the solute moves to the aqueous phase. K, which describes the neutral base, does not change.
